questions.q: What is the primary purpose of sensory imagery in a descriptive passage like "Coorg"?
questions.a: The primary purpose is to create a vivid, immersive experience for the reader by appealing to the five senses, thereby building a dominant impression of the place. A wrong answer (e.g., "to give factual information about coffee production") reveals the student is treating the text as an informational report rather than a literary description — a common error that leads to missing marks for "analysis of language" in the marking scheme.

questions.q: The author writes: "The air is heavy with the scent of coffee." Identify the sense appealed to and explain the effect of the word "heavy."
questions.a: The sense is smell (olfactory). "Heavy" suggests the scent is intense, pervasive, and almost tangible, conveying the richness of the coffee blossoms and the all-encompassing nature of the plantation atmosphere. A wrong answer that only says "smell" without explaining "heavy" shows the student can label the device but cannot analyze its connotation — a skill explicitly tested in CBSE competency questions.

questions.q: In the passage, the river Kaveri is described as "flowing gently" and "full of mahaseer." If you were asked to compare the mood created by the river description with the mood of the coffee plantation description, what two contrasting moods would you identify and which phrases support each?
questions.a: The coffee plantation evokes a lush, aromatic, almost sensual mood (phrases: "heavy with the scent," "rolling hills," "primeval forest"). The river evokes a calm, serene, life-sustaining mood (phrases: "flows gently," "full of mahaseer," "kingfisher dives"). A wrong answer that lists the same mood for both (e.g., "both are beautiful") reveals an inability to distinguish nuanced tonal shifts — a key analytic skill for 3-mark questions.

questions.q: The author mentions "wild elephants," "macaques," "squirrels," and "langurs" in quick succession. Why does the author choose this specific list of animals rather than just saying "wildlife is abundant"?
questions.a: The specific list creates concrete visual imagery, shows biodiversity (different species, sizes, behaviors), and implies a balanced ecosystem — each animal occupies a different niche. Simply saying "abundant wildlife" would be vague and tell, not show. A wrong answer that says "to make it interesting" misses the analytical point: the list functions as evidence for the dominant impression of an untouched, thriving natural habitat.

questions.q: Evaluate this student claim: "The Coorg passage is just a travel brochure — it only lists pretty things to attract tourists." Defend or refute using evidence from the text.
questions.a: Refute. A travel brochure uses persuasive, exaggerated language ("must-visit," "paradise"). The passage uses objective, sensory observation ("rainforests cover thirty percent," "the climb to the Brahmagiri hills") and includes ecological details (mahaseer, kingfisher) that serve an informative, appreciative purpose, not a commercial one. The author's tone is reverent, not promotional. A wrong answer that agrees reveals a confusion between genre (literary description vs. advertisement) and an inability to detect authorial tone.

questions.q: Write a 4-line descriptive paragraph about a hill station you have visited, using at least three different senses and one metaphor, modeled on the style of the Coorg passage.
questions.a: A strong answer will include: (1) visual detail (e.g., "mist clung to pine slopes"), (2) olfactory detail (e.g., "air scented with damp earth and pine resin"), (3) auditory detail (e.g., "a stream's whisper over stones"), and (4) a metaphor (e.g., "the hills were sleeping giants wrapped in green blankets"). A poor answer that only lists sights ("I saw mountains, trees, a river") shows the student cannot transfer the skill of multi-sensory description to their own writing — a gap that hurts both literature and writing-section performance.
